strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: principled online RL training of discrete diffusion policies for combinatorial action spaces, filling a gap relative to the well-studied continuous-diffusion-RL literature.

The core methodological idea—casting the PMD policy-improvement step as a distributional-matching problem and deriving tractable forward-KL (ELBO-weighted self-imitation) and reverse-KL (via ELBO-difference or single-step augmented-MDP importance ratios) objectives—is theoretically motivated, with derivations and proofs provided in the appendix.

Broad and diverse experimental validation across three qualitatively different domains: single-step reward fine-tuning (DNA sequences), long-horizon macro-action RL (MinAtar/Atari), and cooperative multi-agent RL (Google Research Football), demonstrating the generality of the framework.

Useful practical contributions beyond the core algorithm: on-policy diffusion training to align training/inference distributions, a principled temperature auto-tuning scheme via Lagrangian duality, and inference-time sampling techniques (top-p, remasking) that improve efficiency for long macro-actions.
Reasonably thorough ablations (architecture, on-policy training, temperature tuning, sampling technique, scalability vs. macro-action length) that support the design choices.
Reports efficiency gains over the DRAKES baseline (substantially lower GPU memory and wall-clock time) which strengthens the practical significance claim.
weaknesses: Several headline results show implausibly large improvement factors (e.g., RL-D2 achieving 178.9K±64.6K vs. ~1.1K for the best baseline on Space Invaders, or 20.18K±3.75K vs. ~300 on Breakout in Table 1), which is at minimum under-explained and raises concerns about experimental fairness, potential differences in effective action-space definitions, or measurement artifacts; the paper does not investigate or justify why gains of this magnitude occur.

The comparison between the macro-action diffusion policy and single-step baselines (DQN, IMPALA, PPO, R2D2) in Fig. 2/Table 5 conflates the benefit of macro-action commitment itself with the benefit of the diffusion parameterization; while DQN-Macro/IMPALA-Macro control for macro-actions to some degree, the gap between RL-D2 and these macro baselines is still enormous and not sufficiently analyzed (e.g., no controlled study isolating representation power from action horizon effects).

Reported variances are very large in many settings with only 3 random seeds, which is a thin basis for statistical confidence on high-variance Atari benchmarks, and no significance testing is reported.

Reverse KL divergence relies on two approximate importance-sampling ratio estimators (biased ELBO-difference and single-step augmented-MDP ratio) whose bias/variance tradeoffs are not empirically compared or quantified, despite this being central to the RKL variant used in the MARL experiments.

No overall convergence or sample-complexity guarantee is given for the proposed algorithm despite building on PMD theory that provides such guarantees in the tabular/regularized setting; the theoretical contribution is limited to KL-bound derivations rather than end-to-end guarantees for the diffusion-parameterized policy.

Presentation has multiple rough edges: a broken/incomplete citation and sentence ("()zekri2025fine", the abrupt cutoff "We only need to change" in Appendix C.3), garbled/duplicated bibliography entries, and generally dense notation that could benefit from a cleaner main-text summary of the algorithm (e.g., pseudocode for the main training loop is missing from the main paper, only appearing implicitly).

No mention of code/data release or artifact availability, which limits reproducibility given the many implementation-specific choices (network architectures, hyperparameters, importance-ratio estimator selection per domain) documented only in extensive appendices.

Baselines for the Atari/MinAtar macro-action experiments are relatively dated (DQN, IMPALA, PPO, R2D2); no comparison to more recent or stronger sequence-model-based macro-action policies (e.g., autoregressive transformer policies, as used for the football experiments) is included in the Atari section, weakening the case that expressiveness specifically from diffusion (rather than any expressive sequence model) is responsible for gains.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: how to train expressive generative (discrete diffusion) policies online via RL in large combinatorial action spaces, moving beyond autoregressive or factorized-action approaches.

The theoretical construction is relatively complete: they derive both a forward-KL (ELBO-weighted self-imitation) and a reverse-KL (PMD-equivalent, PPO-style clipped) policy-improvement rule from the PMD target distribution, with proofs provided in the appendix, and connect the forward-KL limit to classification-based policy iteration.

The experimental scope is broad, spanning three qualitatively different settings (single-step DNA sequence reward optimization, long-horizon macro-action Atari/MinAtar, and cooperative multi-agent Google Research Football), which is a reasonable way to stress-test generality of the method.

Useful practical techniques are proposed and ablated, such as on-policy diffusion training to align the ELBO training distribution with the inference-time generative process, and inference-time efficiency tricks (top-p sampling, remasking) for long macro-action sequences.

Reported efficiency gains against the DRAKES baseline on DNA generation (lower GPU memory and runtime by not backpropagating through the full reverse chain) are a credible and practically relevant advantage of the proposed decoupled FKL objective.
weaknesses: Several of the headline Atari/MinAtar numbers look implausible or are not sanity-checked: e.g., RL-D2's Breakout score of 20.18K (Table 1) and Space Invaders scores in the hundreds of thousands (178.9K, Table 1; 802.99K in Berzerk, Table 5) vastly exceed typical reported ranges for these games in the literature, which raises concern about whether macro-action score accounting (e.g., reward accumulation over K repeated/combined primitive actions) is being compared fairly against the single-action baselines, rather than reflecting a genuine capability gap.

The abstract and conclusion claim 'state-of-the-art results' and superior performance 'across a diverse set of challenging combinatorial benchmarks' in all settings, but the full Atari results (Table 5/Fig. 6) show RL-D2 wins in only 36 of 56 games, i.e., loses in over a third of environments; this overclaiming in the abstract is not adequately qualified in the main text.

The MARL evaluation (Section 5.3) compares against a single autoregressive-transformer baseline (Wen et al., 2022b) only; no comparison to well-established MARL baselines (e.g., QMIX, MAPPO, HAPPO) is provided, which weakens the significance of the Google Research Football results and makes it hard to assess whether gains stem from the diffusion parameterization or simply from a stronger base architecture/training setup than the one baseline chosen.

The paper's writing and reference list contain clear errors suggesting insufficient proofreading: a broken/garbled citation '()zekri2025fine', a duplicated Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015 reference, a garbled Unicode URL in the Wen et al. 2022a reference, and a hyperparameter table (Table 3) that lists 'Diffusion steps' with value 'Num of players' seemingly copy-pasted from the GRF table (Table 4) rather than an actual Atari-relevant value.

The reverse-KL importance-sampling ratio estimator based on ELBO differences is explicitly acknowledged as biased (Appendix B.3), but the bias term Γ(s,a;θ) is never empirically quantified or bounded, and no ablation compares this estimator against the 'single-step ratio' alternative to justify when each is preferable beyond an informal statement that RKL 'worked best' for MARL.

Core experiments rely on only 3 random seeds, and confidence intervals in several tables are very large relative to the reported means (e.g., Space Invaders ±64.63K on a 178.9K score), undermining confidence in the statistical significance of the claimed improvements.

The core algorithmic idea is essentially a combination of existing components (policy mirror descent targets + discrete/masked diffusion ELBO objectives + standard PPO-clipping for the RKL variant), and the forward-KL objective is explicitly identified as a generalization of a known classification-based policy iteration method (Lazaric et al., 2016); the degree of genuine methodological novelty beyond assembling known pieces for a new application is therefore moderate.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: no code release is mentioned, and baseline tuning procedures (e.g., whether DQN-Macro, IMPALA-Macro, PPO, R2D2 baselines received comparable hyperparameter search effort as RL-D2) are not described, making it difficult to assess whether the large reported margins reflect a fair comparison.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework (RL-D2) that connects policy mirror descent with discrete diffusion models, framing policy improvement as a distributional matching problem; this decoupling of RL optimization and representation learning is a clean and principled idea.

Solid theoretical derivations: the paper derives tractable forward-KL (self-imitation/ELBO-weighted) and reverse-KL (PPO-style with importance ratio approximations) objectives, with proofs provided in the appendix connecting them back to the PMD objective.

Broad and diverse experimental validation across three very different domains (DNA sequence generation, long-horizon Atari with macro-actions, and cooperative multi-agent football), which strengthens the generality claim of the method.

Strong empirical performance: state-of-the-art reward/log-likelihood trade-off on DNA generation with large computational savings over DRAKES (GPU memory 66.4GB->10.6GB, time 268min->97min), and clear improvements over macro-action baselines and autoregressive transformers in Atari and GRF.

Useful practical techniques and ablations: temperature auto-tuning via a KL-constrained dual formulation, on-policy diffusion training, top-p/remasking sampling strategies, and architecture (transformer vs MLP) ablations, which aid reproducibility and practical adoption.

Scalability analysis with macro-action length (2 to 32/50) and compute (model size, samples, wall-time) that illustrates how the diffusion policy avoids the combinatorial blow-up that cripples DQN/IMPALA variants.
weaknesses: Some reported performance gaps are extremely large and somewhat suspicious (e.g., RL-D2 scoring 20.18K vs. DQN-Macro's 300 on Breakout, or 178.9K vs. 1.12K on Space Invaders with very large confidence intervals), raising questions about baseline tuning fairness, potential differences in network capacity/compute budget across methods, or reward-scale artifacts that are not fully addressed in the main text.

The paper only outperforms baselines in 36 of 56 full Atari environments, yet the abstract and conclusion claim 'state-of-the-art results' broadly; a more nuanced, env-by-env discussion of where/why the method underperforms would improve rigor.

Key reverse-KL importance-sampling estimators (ELBO-difference ratio and single-step ratio) are acknowledged as biased approximations, but the practical impact/magnitude of this bias is not empirically quantified or ablated, leaving open how much it affects policy improvement guarantees in practice.

Statistical robustness is limited: only 3 seeds are used for the Atari/MinAtar/GRF experiments, and some confidence intervals are very wide relative to the mean (e.g., Space Invaders ±64.63K), making it hard to assess the reliability/significance of the headline comparisons.

The multi-agent football section only compares against a single autoregressive baseline (Wen et al. 2022b), omitting other common/strong MARL baselines (e.g., QMIX, MAPPO, factorized value baselines), limiting the strength of the significance claims in that domain.

Presentation has multiple rough edges: a broken citation ('()zekri2025fine'), a duplicated reference (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 appears twice), and garbled author/URL text in the Wen et al. reference, suggesting the manuscript needs another proofreading pass before publication.

The combinatorial action-space formulation requires imposing an arbitrary fixed ordering on components (e.g., agents in MARL), which is similar in spirit to the causal-ordering limitation the paper criticizes in autoregressive baselines; this tension is not fully discussed.

No explicit statement about code/data release for reproducibility is provided, despite the detailed hyperparameter tables; given the complexity of the pipeline (distributed RL, diffusion training, PMD target estimation), independent reproduction may be difficult without released code.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously unexplored gap: principled online RL training of discrete diffusion policies for combinatorial action spaces, via a clean theoretical connection to policy mirror descent (target distribution derived analytically, then approximated via FKL/RKL distributional matching).
Both FKL and RKL update rules are derived with formal proofs (Appendix B) connecting them back to the PMD objective, giving the method a principled foundation rather than being purely heuristic.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across three qualitatively different combinatorial domains: single-step DNA sequence generation (bandit), long-horizon Atari with macro-actions, and cooperative multi-agent joint-action learning in Google Research Football — this breadth is unusual and strengthens claims of generality.

Careful baseline design: naive exponential-output (DQN-Macro) and factored (IMPALA-Macro) adaptations, autoregressive joint-action baselines, and strong domain SOTA (DRAKES, MAT, MAPPO) directly test the paper's core hypotheses about combinatorial scaling and causal-order bias.

Rich ablation studies (temperature auto-tuning via KL-constrained duality, on-policy diffusion training, sampling strategies such as top-p and remasking, network architecture, planning with diffusion) that substantively probe design choices rather than just reporting headline numbers.

Good methodological rigor in statistical reporting (stratified bootstrap CIs over 168 Atari runs) and honest discussion of a real FKL/RKL trade-off (sample efficiency vs. asymptotic stability), including reporting failure modes (e.g., FKL collapse under poor temperature tuning, RKL failure in the low-sample GRF regime).
Demonstrated practical efficiency gains over a strong reward fine-tuning baseline (DRAKES) in GPU memory and wall-clock time for the DNA task.
weaknesses: The FKL loss relies on a self-normalized importance-weighted approximation of the softmax reweighting over a small sampled action subset (Appendix B.1); no bias/variance analysis is provided for this approximation in truly large combinatorial spaces, despite this being central to the method's tractability.

The RKL importance ratio uses a single-step augmented-MDP approximation (borrowed from Ren et al. 2024) whose approximation quality/bias relative to the true sequence-level likelihood ratio is not analyzed, only justified empirically.

Mixed/underwhelming results in places undercut the 'state-of-the-art' framing: in MinAtar (Table 1) RL-D2 is not best in 3 of 5 games (Asterix, Seaquest), and RKL fails outright (0.0 win rate) in the low-budget 11v11 GRF ablation—these are honestly reported but somewhat at odds with strong claims in the abstract/intro.

No theoretical convergence or sample-complexity guarantees are given for the practical FKL/RKL algorithms; the PMD convergence theory cited is for the idealized target, not the diffusion-approximated policy update actually used.

Limited comparison to other expressive policy parameterizations for combinatorial actions (e.g., factored/structured generative models, other non-causal generative classes) beyond autoregressive transformers, making it harder to isolate whether gains stem specifically from the diffusion parameterization versus the PMD-based training scheme itself.
Hyperparameter search for baselines is fairly limited (only shown for DQN-Macro), raising some concern about whether other baselines (IMPALA-Macro, MAT, MAPPO) were tuned as thoroughly as RL-D2.

The broader impact/ethics statement is minimal and generic, offering no substantive discussion despite the method's applicability to real-world systems like recommendation and multi-agent coordination.

No explicit mention of code release, which combined with the complexity of the training pipeline (distributed RL infrastructure, custom augmented-MDP ratios, temperature tuning) raises reproducibility concerns despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: parameterizing RL policies over combinatorial discrete action spaces with expressive discrete diffusion models, rather than restrictive factorized or autoregressive representations.

The policy-mirror-descent-as-target-distribution framing is a reasonably principled way to turn policy improvement into a stable distributional matching problem, and the paper provides derivations (Appendix B) connecting FKL/RKL losses to tractable ELBO-based surrogates.
Experiments span three genuinely different domains (DNA sequence generation, long-horizon Atari with macro-actions, and cooperative multi-agent football), which is a broad and ambitious evaluation.

Numerous ablations are included (temperature auto-tuning via a KL-constrained dual derivation, on-policy diffusion training, sampling techniques such as top-p/remasking, network architecture, scalability with macro-action length), and statistical treatment of Atari results uses stratified bootstrap confidence intervals.
Reported computational efficiency gains over DRAKES (memory and wall-clock) are a concrete practical benefit for the DNA task.
weaknesses: Several headline improvements are implausibly large (e.g., Breakout 20.58K vs. next-best baseline ~316, Space Invaders 184.3K vs. ~1.16K, near-ceiling 97-99% win rates on GRF vs. 60-95% for MAT/MAPPO), which raises concerns about whether baselines (DQN-Macro, IMPALA-Macro, MAT, MAPPO) were tuned as carefully as the proposed method; no baseline-specific hyperparameter search is reported except for DQN-Macro.

The macro-action baselines are simple/naive adaptations (direct |A|^K output head or independent per-slot logits) rather than stronger structured baselines (e.g., option-critic, factorized/autoregressive Q-decomposition, hierarchical RL methods), making the comparison less convincing as evidence that diffusion specifically—rather than any more capable architecture—is responsible for gains.

The tractable 'single-step ratio' importance-sampling construction for RKL (borrowed from Ren et al. 2024) substitutes a per-denoising-step ratio for the intractable full-trajectory likelihood ratio; the paper does not rigorously justify the bias/variance implications of this approximation, despite noting empirically that RKL requires larger batches due to 'high-variance nature of the augmented MDP method.'

No formal argument connects the diffusion ELBO surrogate objectives back to the provable convergence guarantees of policy mirror descent; the theoretical PMD guarantees are cited as motivation but the practical algorithm optimizes a looser bound (FKL) or an approximate ratio (RKL), leaving the stability/convergence claims largely empirical.

Directly relevant diffusion-RL baselines cited in related work (DPPO/Ren et al. 2024, Ding et al. 2024, Ma et al. 2025) are not empirically compared against, despite being close competitors conceptually.

Some internal results appear inconsistent with the paper's own motivating narrative (e.g., DQN outperforms DQN-Macro on Asterix and Seaquest in Table 1), which is not discussed and undercuts the claim that macro-actions plus the proposed policy class are uniformly beneficial.

The Impact Statement is a boilerplate dismissal ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted') despite the paper explicitly targeting DNA/enhancer sequence design and recommender-system-style slate generation, both of which carry plausible dual-use or societal considerations that merit at least brief discussion.
No mention of code or data release, limiting reproducibility despite the extensive hyperparameter tables in the appendix.

The abstract's claim of 'state-of-the-art results' is only partially supported once individual task-level results are examined (e.g., MinAtar Asterix/Seaquest), suggesting some overstatement of generality of the improvements.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and reasonably novel framework (RL-D2) that connects policy mirror descent theory with discrete diffusion model training, turning the RL policy-improvement step into a tractable distributional-matching problem via forward/reverse KL objectives.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across three genuinely different combinatorial-action domains (DNA sequence generation, Atari with macro-actions, and cooperative MARL in Google Research Football), which strengthens claims of general applicability.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance versus multiple relevant baselines (DRAKES, DQN/IMPALA-Macro, MAT/MAPPO, autoregressive samplers), including favorable computational efficiency comparisons (e.g., large GPU memory/time reduction versus DRAKES).

Thoughtful ablation studies covering FKL vs. RKL trade-offs, temperature auto-tuning via hard KL constraints, on-policy diffusion training, sampling techniques (top-p, remasking), scalability with macro-action length, and network architecture choices.
Careful statistical reporting using stratified bootstrap confidence intervals across many seeds/tasks, and fairly detailed hyperparameter/appendix documentation that aids reproducibility.
Derivations for the FKL and RKL losses are provided with proofs in the appendix, giving the method some theoretical grounding beyond pure heuristics.
weaknesses: The forward-KL objective is only a tractable upper bound (via the diffusion ELBO and subsampled action sets), so the strong empirical FKL results lack the same theoretical improvement guarantees claimed for RKL; the practical algorithm deviates non-trivially from the idealized PMD target, and this gap is not deeply analyzed.

The RKL importance-sampling ratio construction (augmented MDP over diffusion steps, single-step ratio) is adapted directly from prior work (Ren et al., 2024) on continuous diffusion policies, somewhat limiting the originality of this component.

Some result framing is optimistic: e.g., in MinAtar (Table 1) RL-D2 only wins in 2 of 5 games and is clearly outperformed by DQN in Asterix and by DQN-Macro in Seaquest, yet the narrative emphasizes RL-D2's superiority; likewise in Atari, RL-D2 loses on roughly 20/56 games, which is understated in the main text relative to the state-of-the-art framing.

Baseline tuning appears asymmetric — a hyperparameter search is performed for DQN-Macro but not explicitly for IMPALA-Macro or other adapted baselines, raising some concern about fairness of comparisons.

No substantive discussion of limitations or failure modes in the main text (e.g., when diffusion policies underperform, sensitivity to temperature/KL-constraint schedules causing collapse as shown in the appendix, or scaling limits of the fixed-length sequence assumption for genuinely variable-size combinatorial actions); the Impact Statement is a boilerplate placeholder with no engagement with limitations or ethical considerations.

The method has many interacting design choices (PMD target, FKL/RKL choice, temperature schedule, on-policy diffusion training, sampling technique) each requiring careful tuning, which may hinder practical reproducibility and adoption despite the appendix ablations.

Comparisons are largely against classical or autoregressive baselines; there is limited comparison against other recent discrete-diffusion-policy or discrete generative RL methods beyond DRAKES, leaving open how RL-D2 compares to a broader landscape of emerging discrete diffusion RL approaches.
